extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and academic researchers (faculty, postdocs, graduate students) concerned with journals, conferences, seminars, and academic publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for mathematical conferences, seminars, journals (especially open-access), online talks, and general academic-life practices. Covers how to judge journals (editorial board, peer review, APCs), how to run/attend seminars and conferences, and recommended author practices (posting to arXiv, profiles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk delivery quality at conferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reading your paper to yourself in a monotone; speak to the audience and be engaging rather than rushed, hesitating, bored, tedious and incomprehensible (Charlotte Angas Scott's criticism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good talks address the audience, use clear pacing and engagement. Anti-pattern: reading verbatim in monotone, which makes lectures tedious and incomprehensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invited-speaker pedagogical training
rubrics_metrics.description: Invited speakers should undergo some sort of teacher-training or 'training camp' to improve presentation skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested where many invited talks are poorly delivered. Training would reduce monotonous, hurried, or tedious presentations and improve audience comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of giant in-person congress format
rubrics_metrics.description: Large ICM-style in-person congresses are often disproportionate to their utility: talks are hard to see, there are usually no questions, and meaningful person-to-person interaction is minimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider moving talks online where they can be watched live or later, be posted for asynchronous viewing, and be accessible across time zones. Environmental (CO2) and accessibility concerns also argued against massive in-person formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of online talks/recordings
rubrics_metrics.description: Online talks that are recorded and posted (e.g., YouTube) allow people to watch live or later, speed up playback, and increase accessibility across time zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: improved accessibility, ability to rewatch/fast-forward, broader participation. Limitations: reduced live interaction and informal networking compared to small workshops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of small, informal workshops
rubrics_metrics.description: Small workshops (e.g., Oberwolfach, AIM, Banff) provide intense interactions and advanced lectures that are irreplaceable and should be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While large-scale meetings may move online, keep small, intimate workshops in-person when possible because they foster meaningful person-to-person interactions and deep collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of society business from publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional societies (e.g., AMS) should separate society governance/business activities from their publishing arms, since business models tied to journals/books can create conflicts and conservative incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary when a society's finances depend on publishing revenue; this can hinder reforms and reduce perceived neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal indexing and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal's absence from MathSciNet and ZbMath is a significant negative signal when evaluating its legitimacy and standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion in established bibliographic services is an important criterion beyond raw impact factor numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact factor is insufficient evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact factor (IF) numbers alone do not prove legitimacy; journals can manipulate metrics or achieve high IF via selected strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use IF cautiously and complement it with other signals (peer review quality, editorial standards, indexing, testimonials). Beware of apparently strong IF growth that may be due to strategic practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial-board composition and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Large numbers of editors (e.g., 800+ editors) or many obscure/nominal board members, or names listed without clear consent, are red flags about editorial quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether known, active experts list the role on their CVs; suspect lists padded by acquaintances, friends, or nominal editors. Editorial board size should plausibly cover the scope of the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence and handling of special issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Proliferation of special issues and aggressive solicitation of guest editors can indicate a business model focused on volume and APC revenues rather than selectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check how special issues are organized, guest-editor vetting, and whether APCs are waived to attract high-profile authors for metric boosting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed of editorial decisions vs review rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Very fast decisions (days) suggest superficial peer review or an editorial model optimized for throughput rather than careful assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer, careful review (months) is not a perfect signal but rapid turnarounds paired with other red flags (random refereeing, vouchers) indicate lower-quality review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-refereeing practices and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Robust peer review requires appropriate referee selection, reasonable time for reports, and substantive feedback; red flags include random assignment to unfamiliar referees, two-week deadlines, superficial reports, and referee vouchers that create perverse incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask about reviewer selection, review timelines, whether reviews are substantive, and whether incentives (vouchers) bias the process toward reciprocity rather than rigorous critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: APC model and financial incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: High article-processing charges (APCs) coupled with high volume create incentives to accept more papers for revenue; the APC-based business model can monetize mediocre work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether APCs are commensurate with editorial and production quality. Consider institutional costs (libraries/grants) and whether the journal's model rewards selectivity or throughput.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiving APCs strategically to boost metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals that waive APCs for highly-cited authors to secure their papers and thus raise citation metrics are engaging in metric-gaming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of journals that disproportionately attract papers from high-h-index authors via waivers intended to boost IF; this can distort perceived quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation/spam and guest-editor recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass emailing academics to serve as guest editors or to submit to special issues is a warning sign of aggressive volume-driven practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate journals solicit purposefully; widespread unsolicited invitations across fields suggest predatory/parasitic behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting and bibliographic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Poor typesetting and forced or bizarre bibliography/style demands (e.g., absurdly enumerated references) indicate weak production standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors' complaints about bibliography style battles or typesetting issues can signal low editorial attention to quality and production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between predatory, parasitic, and legitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all questionable journals fit the classic 'predatory' mold; some operate as 'parasitic' outlets that offer services authors want (fast publication, indexing) while degrading peer review and wasting institutional funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nuanced judgment: collect testimonials from authors/referees, examine editorial and review practices, and consider broader systemic harms (grant/library spending) rather than only whether money was solicited deceptively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting author/referee testimonials as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Real-world testimonials from authors and referees provide critical insight into a journal's practices that metrics cannot reveal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a journal, directly query past authors about invitations, payment, review duration, and experience with production to form a grounded view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional policy responses to APCs
rubrics_metrics.description: Libraries and granting agencies should consider policies limiting use of funds for APCs and reconsider paying for open-access APCs to disincentivize low-quality APC-for-acceptance models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include libraries stopping APC payments, grants disallowing funds for APCs, and promoting arXiv-overlay or other low-cost dissemination models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should post papers openly
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must make their papers freely available (arXiv or personal website) regardless of publisher paywalls; publishers generally permit authors to post their own copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posting improves accessibility, helps readers without subscriptions, and reduces dependence on publishers' access. Keep a clean and updated Google Scholar profile and personal website with papers, slides, and video links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain bibliographic and professional profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use databases like MathSciNet and Zentralblatt, keep Google Scholar current, and maintain your personal website with up-to-date publications and materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tidy online presence helps visibility and avoids misattribution; it takes little time but matters to others evaluating you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights negotiation in book contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: When signing book contracts, retain rights to display a public copy on your website to allow teaching and dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate display rights to support teaching and accessibility; refusing to share short sections can make your work less useful to colleagues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage camera-on behavior for online seminars
rubrics_metrics.description: Seminar organizers should encourage participants to turn on cameras to give speakers visual feedback (nodding, quizzing) that helps pacing and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple tactic: address only those whose faces are visible. This improves interaction and reduces speaker uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online seminar moderation to foster interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Online seminars suffer from shy audiences and fewer interruptions; organizers must adopt strategies to prompt questions and informal engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record seminars, host post-talk informal meetings, solicit questions in chat, and create spaces for junior colleagues to connect with speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference format trade-offs (online vs in-person)
rubrics_metrics.description: Online conferences reduce travel costs, broaden access, and remove geographic constraints, while in-person meetings remain valuable for networking and small-workshop intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider hybrid approaches: keep small in-person workshops; move large extravaganzas online; re-think expensive meetings that primarily serve as social/ceremonial events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic teaching quality and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Online teaching often requires more preparation, may reduce learning, and increases cheating; instructors should read evaluations and adapt to improve quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take student feedback seriously, invest in course design and technology, and expect some standardization of online teaching requirements while mitigating cheating risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home computing and lecture production
rubrics_metrics.description: Good home computing setup (camera, lighting, mic, whiteboard alternatives) materially affects the quality of online teaching and talks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest prudently in equipment and workflows that worked well; learn from 2020 experiences to improve future remote teaching and presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentoring and collegial responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Be supportive of junior colleagues who may be disadvantaged by online formats and difficult job markets; help them with visibility and opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical actions include inviting junior researchers to speak, sharing resources, and being mindful of inequality exacerbated by remote formats.
